title: Not everything is kamma
hookLine: asked whether all feeling comes from past deeds, the Buddha says no: weather, illness and more play a part (SN 36.21)
last: PHALA — CHILIES DON'T GROW INTO MELONS.

lines: WHAT DID I DO TO DESERVE THIS?
cards: Someone you love gets sick. And sooner or later, someone says it, kindly or not: it must be their karma. Maybe something from a past life.
Sometimes the sick person says it about themselves, lying awake at three in the morning: what did I do to deserve this? The idea gets pinned on Buddhism.
The Buddha was asked about it directly, by a wandering ascetic named Sivaka, and his answer isn't the one the question expects.

teach.b: Sivaka puts it plainly. Some teachers say that whatever a person feels, pleasant, painful or neither, is all caused by what they did in the past. What do you say?
The Buddha says no, and gives a list. Some feelings, Sivaka, arise from bile. Some from phlegm.
Some from wind, which in the medicine of his day meant the body's inner airs. Some from a mix of these. Some from a change of season, the weather.
Some from careless behavior, how a person treats their own body. Some from assault, what someone else does to you. And some from the ripening of kamma.
Eight causes. Kamma is one of them.
Then he says something sharp about the teachers who claim it's all past deeds: they go beyond what a person can know for themselves, and beyond what the world agrees is true.
Anyone can see that a cold snap brings on aches.

So kamma is real in this teaching, and it isn't the whole explanation. Later Buddhist thinkers worked out in detail how kamma and other conditions weave together, and they don't all draw the lines in the same place.
But the sutta's practical point is hard to miss. By this text, telling a sick person their illness is simply their own past doing claims to know what no one in the room can know.
The response that fits the sutta is the one a good doctor and a good friend would give anyway: let's look after you.

how: Buddhist communities visit and care for the sick, and monks are traditionally invited to chant protective verses for the ill; teachers often cite this sutta to correct the idea that illness is simply a punishment.

o: a strong emotion, like anger or grief
a past-life debt you must now pay off

games.q: what Sivaka heard: tap the pairs.

s: the Buddha taught that every illness comes from past deeds
in SN 36.21 he says that view goes beyond what anyone can know; kamma is one of eight causes.
the Buddha names a change of season as one cause of painful feeling
the weather is on his list of eight.
harm done to you by someone else is on the list
assault is one of the eight causes.

games.q: your friend's mother is seriously ill. someone at the hospital says, "it's her karma." by SN 36.21, what's the fair reply?
o: agree; all feeling comes from past deeds.
no one can know that; kamma is one cause among many.
say it's the family's karma instead.
games.why: the Buddha tells Sivaka that claiming all feeling comes from past kamma oversteps what anyone can know; bodily causes, weather, carelessness and assault count too.

practice: Bring to mind someone who is unwell or struggling right now; it may be you.

If a blaming thought is hiding in the picture, they should have, I should have, it's because, don't argue with it; set it gently to one side, the way you'd move a coat off a chair so someone can sit down.
Then let what's left be simple care, the plain wish that they're looked after, and rest there with the breath.

wordCard.voice: Vedana, feeling. In the Connected Discourses the Buddha names eight causes of feeling, from bile to weather to assault, and kamma is only one.

orig.note: Pali vedanā: feeling, pleasant, painful or neither. SN 36.21 asks where it comes from.

carryVoice: Your line: let's look after you. Kamma is real here, and it isn't the whole story. Take good care.

sources.ref: Milindapañha (the questions of King Milinda, on whether all feeling is kamma)
